bib.title: Archon: An Architecture Search Framework for Inference-Time Techniques

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "An Architecture Search Framework for Inference-Time Techniques" (ARCHON), Jon Saad-Falcon, Adrian Gamarra Lafuente, Shlok Natarajan, Nahum Maru, Hristo Todorov, Etash Guha, E. Kelly Buchanan, Mayee Chen, Neel Guha, Christopher Ré, Azalia Mirhoseini (Stanford, UW). arXiv:2409.15254v6 [cs.LG], 10 Jun 2025. Venue not printed beyond arXiv (preprint/ICML-style template).

COVERAGE: Extracted 126,043 chars, 35 pages. Read main text (pp.1-10), all of appendix A.1-A.10 (pp.16-35: ablation tables 5-9, search-algorithm tables 24-27, benchmark/result tables 28-40, architecture diagrams, prompts). Prompt text (Tables 10-23) only skimmed. References (pp.10-16) skipped except for origins. Extraction clean. No instructions embedded in the PDF. Full text is at /tmp/archon.txt.

TOPOLOGY NOTE: ADAS and AFlow appear only as baselines and in related-work framing. The paper does not describe their search methods. MaAS is not mentioned.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Archon is a layered inference-time architecture (generate, critic, rank, fuse, verify, unit-test) whose configuration is found by Bayesian optimization over a 9,576-point search space. It is explicitly modeled on neural-network layers.
  number: 9,576 configurations (18,750 before pruning invalid ones)
  setup: six axes: top-K generators (1-10), samples per generator (1-5; up to 1000 for CodeContests), fusion layers (1-4), fusers per layer (2-10 step 2), critic+ranker before each fuser, optional verifier/unit-test layer before the last fuser. 20% of each benchmark is used as the dev set for search.
  quote: "In total, our search space contains 9,576 configurations, which we obtain by combining all possible hyperparameters and removing invalid configurations"
  where: p.6 (3.3); A.4.1 p.24-25
- claim: Construction rules fix the topology. Layers are sequential and each layer holds one component type. Generators sit only in layer 1. A Critic must precede a Ranker or Fuser. Ranker, Critic, Verifier and unit-test layers must be alone in their layer. Fusers can be several per layer. Unit-test generator and evaluator occupy consecutive layers. Every layer maps a list of strings to a list of strings, and the first string of the last layer is returned.
  number: none
  setup: rules came from an ablation over 7 benchmarks and 2 model classes
  quote: "1. Only one type of component is allowed in any given layer. 2. Generator components can only be placed in the first layer of ARCHON ; you can place one or more Generators. 3. The Critic must come before a Ranker or a Fuser."
  where: p.5 (3.2)
- claim: Headline result. Best Archon architectures beat frontier single LLMs and other inference-time systems by 15.1% on average, while using fewer calls and tokens than ADAS/AFlow/MoA.
  number: 15.1% avg; 20.0% fewer calls, 15.1% fewer input tokens, 13.5% fewer output tokens
  setup: 7 benchmarks (MT-Bench, AlpacaEval 2.0, Arena-Hard-Auto, MixEval, MixEval-Hard, MATH, CodeContests), evaluated on the held-out 80%. Baselines: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1 405B, o1, MoA, ADAS, AFlow. Temperature 0.7. The 15.1% is from closed-source Archon vs closed-source LMs.
  quote: "ARCHON achieves SOTA performances while using 20.0% less inference calls, 15.1% less input tokens, and 13.5% less output tokens than alternative inference-time architectures"
  where: p.3; p.8
- claim: On the same Table 1, ADAS and AFlow use far more compute than Archon but score lower. Their task-specific search outcomes are roughly matched or beaten by Archon's general-purpose architectures.
  number: ADAS 52 calls, 72,804 input tokens, 44,872 output tokens, $0.63/query; AFlow 48 calls, $0.59; Archon open-source task-specific 44 calls, $0.15; all-source task-specific 39 calls, $0.37
  setup: Table 1, held-out 80%. ADAS CodeContests 23.7%, AFlow 21.1%. Archon all-source task-specific CodeContests 41.4%. ADAS MT-Bench 66.3%, AFlow 62.4%, Archon all-source task-specific 79.5%. ADAS MATH 86.0%, AFlow 84.5%, Archon all-source task-specific 93.5%. MoA is 19 calls, $0.06. The PFLOPs column also differs sharply: ADAS 58.8, AFlow 55.2, Archon open-source 3.1-3.7.
  quote: "ADAS 52 72,804 44,872 58.8 ± 0.3 0.63 ± 0.04 66.3% ±0.7 60.1% ±0.5 85.4% ±0.4 64.2% ±0.2 87.0% ±0.2 86.0% ±0.8 23.7% ±0.3"
  where: Table 1, p.8
- claim: Generalization. A general-purpose Archon architecture keeps 91.7-94.2% of the task-specific Archon score on unseen tasks. Generalized ADAS and AFlow keep only 66.8-73.8%.
  number: Archon 91.7%/93.9%/94.2%; AFlow 70.8%/73.8%/67.0%; ADAS 73.2%/73.3%/66.8% (GPQA Diamond / MMLU / MMLU Pro)
  setup: all-source generalized architecture searched on the 7 benchmarks combined and shuffled, then applied to the unseen tasks. MMLU and MMLU Pro use a 500-query sample. Generalized ARCHON scores 56.1/76.5/71.0 vs task-specific 61.2/81.5/75.4.
  quote: "The generalized ADAS and AFlow architectures only achieve 66% and 74% of their specialized architecture performance, respectively."
  where: Table 2 and text, p.9
- claim: At matched budgets, Archon's searched architectures beat the baselines. Compute restrictions are applied by excluding any architecture over the call, input-token or output-token budget from the search space.
  number: 12.4% higher performance at the same token budget; the generalized all-source Archon is 6.4% better and 31% more token-efficient than the best LM-system baselines
  setup: Figures 5, 8, 9 (FLOP, token and dollar budgets). MoA and o1 are static and so appear as a single point. 10 runs averaged.
  quote: "we find that the generated ARCHON architectures achieve 12.4% higher performance than alternate baselines when given the same budget."
  where: p.7-8 (3.3, 4.2)
- claim: Search method. Bayesian optimization (Gaussian process surrogate, Expected Improvement) finds the best architectures with far fewer evaluations than greedy or random search. It is less useful at small budgets.
  number: best architecture in 96.0% of searches; 88.5% fewer evaluations than greedy and 90.4% fewer than random; 230-240 initial random points optimal; weak below 20 calls
  setup: MT-Bench and Arena-Hard-Auto, space of 9,576. Iterations to convergence on MT-Bench (Table 27): at a budget of 50 calls, random 5843, greedy 4895, Bayes 589. At 10 calls: 387 / 343 / 254. Objective f(x)=Performance(x) − λ·Cost(x).
  quote: "Bayesian optimization found the best architectures in 96.0% of searches and required 88.5% fewer architecture evaluations than greedy search and 90.4% fewer than random search (Figure 10)."
  where: p.6; Table 27 p.27
- claim: The discovered topologies depend on the task. The general architecture is a 10-generator first layer followed by four critique-and-fuse stages whose fuser counts shrink (a "funneling" shape). Math tasks get a wide generation layer reduced quickly to one answer. Coding tasks get repeated generate-critique-fuse over a single response, with unit tests.
  number: funnel of 10 generators, then 10, 8, 6, 4 fusers
  setup: all-source general architecture (Fig 13), instruction-following (Fig 14), math (Fig 15, 5 samples each, GPT-4o verifier), coding (Fig 16, 4 rounds, unit tests)
  quote: "Each subsequent layer has fewer fuser models (i.e. 8, 6, and 4), leading to a \"funneling\" effect on the generations before the final output."
  where: p.8; Figs 13-16 pp.33-34
- claim: Component-level gains (ablations, open-source 70B+ ensemble of the best 8 models). Critic+Ranker+Fuser is the strongest general topology. Fuser alone helps; critic before fuser helps more.
  number: Arena-Hard-Auto raw W.R. 37.1% (best single model) vs 51.3% (Ensemble+Fuser) vs 65.8% (+Critic) vs 72.4% (Ensemble+Critic+Ranker+Fuser, 11 calls)
  setup: Table 5; MT-Bench 55.0 vs 64.7%. Ranker alone is worse than the 10-sample best-model baseline by 3.0 points on average. The same pattern holds with GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Claude 3 Haiku (Tables 6-9).
  quote: "Ensemble + Critic + Ranker + Fuser 11 64.7% ±0.4 62.6% ±0.6 72.4% ±0.5 60.9% ±0.6 66.8% ±0.4 88.3% ±0.2 87.3% ±0.5 25.5% ±0.3"
  where: Table 5, p.19
- claim: Task dependence of components. The fuser helps every benchmark. Layers of fusion help instruction tasks more than MixEval. The verifier and unit tests help reasoning and coding. Ranker works best on style tasks.
  number: Fuser +8.9% avg; Critic +11.5 points (main text; the appendix says +3.1, an inconsistency); Verifier +8.4% on MixEval/MixEval-Hard/MATH; unit tests +7.4%
  setup: 70B+ open-source ensemble. Fuser layers: 1-2 pt gain for MixEval, 10-15 pt win-rate gain for MT-Bench/AlpacaEval 2.0 with 3-4 layers (the appendix says 2-5 pts for the same).
  quote: "The Critic module proved effective for every task we explored in Figure 4 and Table 5. With our 10-model 70B+ Generator ensemble and Fuser configuration of ARCHON , the added Critic improved performance on average by 11.5 percentage points across the benchmarks explored."
  where: p.3-4; A.3.3 p.18
- claim: Coding needs sampling plus unit tests, not ensembling and fusion. Unit tests plus heavy sampling lifted CodeContests Pass@1.
  number: 17.9% to 29.3% Pass@1 (+56%); GPT-4o 40 to 58 of 140 questions (+44.3%)
  setup: CodeContests, 140 non-image test problems. One model dominates (Llama 3.1 405B). 5 unit tests are generated per query. Task-specific all-source reaches 41.4%.
  quote: "we observed a 56% boost in Pass@1 performance (Table 1), increasing from 17.9 to 29.3% Pass@1."
  where: p.4; p.9
- claim: More models in the ensemble and more samples both help. Ensemble size gives the larger gain. Ensemble fusion beats fusing repeated samples from a single model.
  number: +9.3% from repeated sampling, +18.5% from adding models (Arena-Hard-Auto)
  setup: models added best-to-worst; top-5 ranked then fused scores highest. Jaccard similarity between the fused output and the candidates is lower for the ensemble (e.g. 28.9% on Arena-Hard-Auto) than for 8 samples of one model (48.4%), so the ensemble gives more diverse output.
  quote: "increasing by 9.3% and 18.5%, respectively."
  where: Fig 11 p.28; Table 36 p.32
- claim: Per-subtask architectures help reasoning. Different tasks need different topologies.
  number: +3.7 and +8.9 points (MixEval, MixEval-Hard)
  setup: separate architecture per MixEval sub-dataset (Tables 30-31)
  quote: "we see 3.7 and 8.9 percentage point increases in accuracy, on average, for MixEval and MixEval-Hard, respectively."
  where: p.9
- claim: Cost and latency are high, and the approach needs strong models.
  number: up to 5x time and money of a single call; 7B models give +7.5% over the best single 7B; Archon with 7B models gives limited gains
  setup: Table 39 costs (as of Nov 2024); Table 40 gives $0.19-0.46/query for Archon vs $0.017-0.56 for single LLMs. Task-specific architectures use 15.5% more input and 18.6% more output tokens than general ones, for 8.4% higher accuracy. A 7B ensemble with critic and fusion actually scores below the best single 7B model (Table 38).
  quote: "it can take 5x more time and money than a single LLM API call"
  where: p.9; Tables 38-40 pp.34-35
- claim: Search sensitivity to budget. Gains saturate with call budget.
  number: all-source-style 70B+ MT-Bench 55.0% at 1 call, 71.6% at 50 calls; closed models 45.0% to 80.4%
  setup: Table 37, flat after about 30-40 calls on most tasks
  quote: "70B+ Models 1 55.0% 44.7% 45.6% 86.5% 61.1% ... 50 71.6% 66.7% 69.0% 89.5% 67.5%"
  where: Table 37 p.34

LIMITS
- No dedicated limitations section. The authors concede that Archon is 5x slower and costlier than one call, is most effective with 70B+ models, that Bayesian optimization is weak below about 20 calls, and that ranking math and coding is a challenge ("our findings show the importance of building better rankers for more complex reasoning tasks").
- The search space is fixed and hand-designed: layered, linear, one state, no learned weights, no free-form graphs, no code generation of new components. This differs sharply from ADAS (searches over code) and AFlow (searches over workflows). Text-to-text components only, with no tools or agents.
- Search and evaluation use the same benchmarks (20% dev / 80% held-out). The held-out delta is 0.44% on average. Closed-source baselines (o1) have unknown call counts. All models are from mid-2024 and prices are Nov 2024.
- ADAS and AFlow were compute-matched via restrictions. The paper does not detail how the baselines were run or tuned, and says only that both are "single-model systems".
- Internal inconsistencies between main text and appendix (Critic +11.5 vs +3.1; Ranker +10.8% vs +3.8%; fusion layers 10-15 vs 2-5 pts; the "closed-source 15.1%" and "all-source 10.9%" averages). Treat headline averages with care. The standard errors come from 10 evaluation runs.
- Judges are GPT-4-Turbo/GPT-4-0314, so there is judge bias risk. They added a Claude 3.5 Sonnet reference run for Arena-Hard-Auto (Table 29).

BUILDS ON
Mixture-of-Agents (Wang et al., 2024a); LLM-Blender (Jiang et al., 2023b); Large Language Monkeys (Brown et al., 2024); "Are more LLM calls all you need?" (Chen et al., 2024); Networks of Networks (Davis et al., 2024); Bayesian optimization (Snoek et al., 2012; Nardi et al., 2019); NAS (Zoph & Le, 2017; Ren et al., 2021); DSPy (Khattab et al., 2023); TextGrad (Yuksekgonul et al., 2024); Constitutional AI critiques (Bai et al., 2022); LLM-as-judge (Zheng et al., 2023). Compared against ADAS (Hu et al., 2024) and AFlow (Zhang et al., 2024).

CODE: none in the paper. Prompt templates are in Tables 10-23 (pp.22-24). The search objective is (A.4.1, p.25): "f (x) =Performance(x) − λ · Cost(x)"; acquisition is "EI(x; H) =E[max(0, f(x) − f (x+))]".

FIGURES (not extracted via the captions script; captions are from the text)
- Fig 2 (p.2): framework overview of inputs (benchmarks, call budget, LLMs, techniques), the optimizer, and the output architecture.
- Fig 3 (p.5): example 10-generator, critic, ranker, 6-fuser, verifier, final-fuser stack. Best for showing the layer topology.
- Fig 4 (p.6): performance as layers of critique and fusion are added; the basis for the task-dependent search ("18.8% boost" on average).
- Fig 5 / 8 / 9 (pp.10, 21): accuracy vs FLOP, token and dollar budgets against baselines (Pareto frontier).
- Fig 10 (p.26): search algorithm comparison. Fig 13-16 (pp.33-34): discovered architectures (funnel, instruction, math, coding).

PROBLEMS: No extraction faults. Tables are flattened, but numbers are readable. I did not run the figures script. "Table 1 caption" says the standard error comes from 10 runs. Some table cells contain "N/A" (Claude 3.5 Sonnet on MT-Bench/Arena-Hard-Auto, since it was the reference model).
